newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia stocks mixed as Greenspan reaction fades.
newsitem.headline: Asia stocks mixed as Greenspan reaction fades.

text.p: Asian stocks recovered early losses and were narrowly mixed on Thursday with traders shrugging off U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's warning that interest rates might move higher.
In an uncharacteristically blunt forecast, Greenspan told the Senate Banking Committee on Wednesday that the U.S. central bank might take a pre-emptive shot at fighting inflation.
"It is conceivable...to have to move before you see actual evidences of real inflation emerging," Greenspan said during his bi-annual testimony to Congress.
The comments served as a red flag to Wall Street, where stock and bond prices fell sharply and the dollar rose.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 55 points to 6,983, while the U.S. Treasury's benchmark 30-year bond closed 1-1/2 points lower at 98-3/32 to yield 6.77 percent. The dollar ended slightly above 1.69 marks compared with 1.6747 on Tuesday and at 122.63 yen against 121.20.
Most Asian markets followed Wall Street's lead at the opening, but the "herd instinct" which usually grips markets after a Greenspan speech, failed to take hold.
"The market is not collapsing," said Howard Gorges, a director at South China Brokerage in Hong Kong.
"I think there has been an expectation for some time that Greenspan is itching to find an excuse to put rates up and it is likely to happen sooner rather than later," he said.
Greenspan told the committee he did not see evidence of inflation in the U.S. economy, on which he gave an upbeat assessment.
But he reiterated a warning he made in December about an "irrational exuberance" among stock and bond investors.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was off 27.80 points, or 0.21 percent, at 13,514.03 at the midday break. It had been down more than 100 points earlier.
In Tokyo, the key Nikkei 225-share index was up 30.64 points, or 0.16 percent, at 19,021.56 in afternoon trade after dropping 108 points earlier.
"The Greenspan-inspired drop looks like a one-time thing which provided the market with a chance to bargain hunt," one broker in Tokyo said.
By midday in Tokyo, the dollar had weakened to 121.31 yen but was steady around 1.69 marks.
Trading in the Philippines was suspended and the market subsequently closed by the Stock Exchange after a computer glitch disrupted early trading.

The composite index was off 14.40 points, or 0.43 percent to 3,335.42. Malaysian shares were lower at midday after profit-taking erased early modest gains. The Composite Index was off 6.30 points to 1,259.07.
Singapore's Straits Times Index was down 9.51 points, or 0.43 percent, at midday to 2,206.56, while Thai stocks dropped 6.24 points, or 0.84 percent, to 733.58.
Korean stocks were off 5.70 points, or 0.84 percent, at 674.01 at the break on rumours of financial difficulties at Sammi Corp.
A Sammi executive said the company had missed the first deadline for debt repayments two days ago, but that the firm was able to make up for it the next day.
Indonesian stocks benefited from positive sentiment among local investors and were up 2.14 points, or 0.30 percent, at 714.747 at midday.
Taiwan stocks resumed their advance and ended up 101.58 points, or 1.31 percent, at 7,832.07.
The market had dropped sharply on Wednesday after the government cancelled a planned share offering, sparking fears it would try to cool the red-hot bourse.
But those fears were alleviated after the Stock Exchange said on Thursday that the cancellation was an isolated case.
Australian stocks closed 18.4 points lower at 2,467.7, while New Zealand shares ended down 15.96 points to 2,274.19.
